No, not really. I mean, I still enjoy what I do. Painting and paperhanging, it's—well, it's satisfying, you know? There's this moment when you've prepped a wall perfectly, patched all the little dings and gouges, sanded it smooth, and you lay down that first coat of paint or that first strip of wallpaper, and it just transforms the space. It's just that there's so much of it! I mean, last week I had to read three chapters on the Industrial Revolution, plus a whole separate article on labor movements, and it's just a mountain of text. I still want to learn it, I still care about getting my degree, but it's hard to find the energy to focus when I've been on a ladder for eight hours. So it's not that I don't care or that I've lost interest, it's just... I'm stretched thin. I'm just trying to keep all the plates spinning, you know? It's not a lack of pleasure, it's just a lack of hours in the day and energy in my body.

Well, I mean, as far as my appetite goes, like I said, I just don't have a lot of time to sit around and think about being hungry. When you're in the middle of a big job, you know, measuring out a drop match for a really expensive wallpaper—and let me tell you, if you mess up a drop match, the client is furious because that paper is sometimes a hundred dollars a roll—you just don't even register hunger. It sheds whatever is slowing it down. It's just conditioning. I'm just getting leaner and more efficient for the work I have to do. It's not like I'm trying to lose weight on purpose, it's just a byproduct of my schedule and the physical demands of my job. So, yeah, I'm smaller, but it's just from working hard.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, I wouldn't say I'm *overly* concerned, not in a vain way, you know? It's not about trying to look like a model in a magazine or anything silly like that. It's more about... functionality. Like I was saying, my job is incredibly physical. When you're constantly maneuvering around tight corners with a bucket of paste, or balancing on the very top rung of a ladder—which you're not really supposed to do, but sometimes you just have to reach that one corner of the ceiling molding—you have to be agile. You have to be light on your feet. 

So, yeah, I guess I do think about it, but only in relation to how I function. Like, if one of the guys on the crew actually convinces me to eat a slice of the pizza they order, or if I were to sit down and eat a big, heavy sub sandwich in the middle of the day, I just... I get this really intense, almost panicky feeling. It's hard to describe. It's like this immediate dread that if I eat something heavy like that, I'm going to wake up the next day bigger, and slower, and sluggish. I just picture myself trying to squeeze behind a radiator to smooth down a piece of wallpaper and getting stuck, or feeling too heavy to hustle up and down the scaffolding. 

It's just this fear that the weight will just stick to me instantly and I won't be able to move around the rooms the way I need to. My whole livelihood depends on me being quick and efficient. If I lose that edge, if I get weighed down, I can't keep up the pace. So I guess, sure, my body shape matters to me, but only because it's my tool, you know? It's the most important tool I have for my work, and I just can't afford to let it get soft or heavy.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, honestly, I guess I'm really only here talking to you right now because the doctor at the clinic got so on my case about my eating. I had gone in recently for a completely standard check-up, just to get some medical clearance paperwork signed for my classes, and suddenly they're interrogating me about my meals and making this massive deal out of nothing. They made it sound like I'm doing this all on purpose, like I have some sort of master plan to restrict what I eat, but that's just not reality. 

The reality is that most days I just keep it simple. I have to. My alarm goes off at 4:30 in the morning, so I just grab a large black coffee. Usually I get it from this little corner store near my apartment because they're the only ones open that early, and I'll just drink it in the work van while I'm navigating morning traffic to get to the job site. And then once I'm there, I'm working. I don't have the luxury of taking a full lunch hour like the other contractors do. If I stop to eat a whole meal, the wallpaper paste dries out, or I lose my daylight for seeing the seams on the walls. So I just have maybe a few bites of something between jobs. I'll keep a granola bar or a little baggie of crackers in the glove compartment, and I'll literally just take two or three bites while I'm driving from one client's house to the next. Just enough to keep me going, you know? 

And then by the time I finally get home, I'm just completely drained. I'll usually just make a really small dinner, like maybe a piece of dry toast or a tiny bowl of soup, but half the time I don't even finish it. Especially if I'm busy with class paperwork. I'm taking these business management classes at the community college so I can eventually run my own contracting company instead of just doing the manual labor forever, and the coursework is intense. I'll sit down at my kitchen table with my laptop and all my accounting spreadsheets, and I just get so hyper-focused on finishing my assignments that eating just completely falls off my radar. 

So, yes, the clinic doctor was really pushing the idea that I'm intentionally starving myself because I'm terrified of gaining weight, and like I told you, I *do* worry about getting heavy and slowing down at work. I absolutely do. But my eating habits are really just a product of my schedule. A coffee, a couple bites during the day, a tiny dinner while I do my homework... it's just what fits into my life right now. I don't know why everyone is acting like it's this huge crisis when I'm clearly still functioning and getting everything done.

Oh, gosh, no. No, never. I can't even imagine doing something like that. Honestly, just the thought of sitting down and eating a massive amount of food all at once... it makes my stomach turn just picturing it. I don't even think my body could physically handle it at this point, to be perfectly honest with you. Like, my stomach is so used to just having those little bits of fuel—the coffee, the crackers, maybe that tiny bowl of soup at night—that if I were to suddenly try and eat a huge meal, I think I'd be violently ill. It would just sit there like a rock.

I see the guys I work with do it all the time, though, and it's actually kind of mind-boggling to me. Just last week, we were finishing up this massive Victorian house remodel over in the historic district—beautiful original plaster walls, by the way, but an absolute nightmare to prep and paper over because nothing is perfectly plumb—and the main crew ordered lunch from this local Italian place. They got these giant, heavy meatball subs, just dripping with cheese and grease, and huge sides of fries. I watched Dave, one of the drywall guys, literally inhale this massive sandwich in maybe eight minutes flat. He just wolfed it down. And then he went right back to work! 

If I ate even a quarter of what he ate, I would be completely incapacitated. I'd have to go lay down in the back of my work van. It would just feel so heavy, and like I was saying before, I wouldn't be able to bend over to measure my paper or climb the ladders safely. I'd feel so sluggish and gross. 

Plus, when would I even have the time for something like that? Eating a large amount of food takes time. You have to sit down, you have to completely stop what you're doing. Between getting up at 4:30 in the morning, driving all over town to different sites, managing the actual physical labor all day, and then coming home to stare at accounting spreadsheets for my business classes until midnight... there's just no window in my day where I would ever just sit and gorge myself on food. It doesn't even make sense for my life. So, no, that's definitely not something I do. I just couldn't.

Your brain is so focused on the task. So I guess my appetite is just... efficient. I eat what I need when I absolutely have to. \n\nBut as for my weight, I mean, yeah, I guess things have changed a little bit. When you are staying on your feet for ten hours a day, carrying five-gallon buckets of joint compound up three flights of stairs because the service elevator is broken, your body just naturally adapts. It's not like I'm trying to lose weight on purpose, it's just a byproduct of my schedule and the physical demands of my job. I mean, I wouldn't really call it a fear of becoming "fat" in, like, a cosmetic or vanity kind of way. I don't care about being on a magazine cover. But gaining weight? Yeah... yeah, I guess I do have a pretty intense fear of that. It’s just... it’s almost a physical reaction for me. 

If I even think about eating something heavy, like the pizza those study groups always want to order, or one of those massive, heavy deli sandwiches the drywallers eat on the job site, I get this really intense, panicky feeling in my chest. I just start spiraling, thinking that if I actually sit down and eat that kind of food, I'll wake up the next morning bigger and slower. And in my line of work, being slow is basically a death sentence for your profit margins and your reputation. 

People really underestimate how athletic you have to be to do high-end wallpapering or custom painting. You're not just standing in one spot. You're constantly up and down a six-foot A-frame ladder, sometimes an extension ladder if you're dealing with a vaulted ceiling or a two-story foyer, which is incredibly dangerous if you aren't completely centered. You're carrying cumbersome rolls of paper, you're dodging buckets of paste, and you're constantly twisting and reaching. If I put on weight, if I get bigger, I just know I won't be able to move around the ladders and navigate these tight rooms the way I need to. 

You have to be so incredibly agile to squeeze behind scaffolding or lean over a staircase railing just right to smooth a seam without tearing the paper. If I'm heavier and sluggish from eating all that dense food, I lose my edge. I lose my balance, my speed, my stamina... everything. I need to stay light on my feet so I can pivot and climb and stretch for eight or ten hours a day. So, yes, the thought of gaining weight absolutely terrifies me, it really makes me panic, but it's because of how it would completely ruin my ability to physically do my job and build my business.

It’s all about control. \n\nSo, my eating is just... it's just another part of that system, I guess. When I reach into the glove compartment of the van and grab those crackers I told you about, I know exactly how many I'm going to have. I'll have two, maybe three, just enough to make sure my hands stay perfectly steady for the trim work, and then I fold the baggie back up and put it away. It’s a very conscious decision. I never sit there and feel like, oh no, I can't stop myself, or feel like the food is somehow controlling me. \n\nAnd as for eating even smaller amounts and feeling like I can't control that... no, I don't think so. I mean, the amounts are small, sure, like the clinic doctor kept loudly pointing out to me, but it's just what I've figured out works for my schedule. I don't feel like it's slipping out of my hands or that I'm being forced to do it. It's just... it's just my routine. I have my coffee, I have my couple of bites, I have my dry toast while I'm doing my accounting homework. It’s all very structured. \n\nHonestly, with everything else in my life being so chaotic right now—juggling the contracting jobs, dealing with suppliers who are always late delivering materials, and trying to pass these heavy business management courses so I can actually get my company off the ground next year—knowing exactly what and when I'm going to eat is one of the few things I actually *do* have total control over. It's predictable. So, no, I don't ever feel out of control with it. Not at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you judge yourself primarily in terms of your body weight or shape, even if others may not see the same things you do?\n\nPatient: Judge myself? Like, my worth as a person? Um, no. No, I really wouldn't say that. I mean, I know I mentioned earlier that I worry about getting heavy because I don't want to slow down on the job site, and that's true, I definitely need to stay light on my feet for the ladders and the scaffolding. But if you're asking what I *primarily* judge myself on, it's definitely not what I look like in a mirror or what a scale says. \n\nHonestly, I judge myself on my work. My work is everything right now. Like, just the other day, I was installing this incredibly delicate grasscloth wallpaper for a client—grasscloth is notoriously unforgiving, by the way, because if you get even a single drop of water or paste on the face of the paper, it stains permanently and you have to scrap the whole panel, which is a total disaster when the client only ordered exactly enough yardage for the room and it's on a six-week backorder. Anyway, I spent eight hours making sure every single seam in that dining room was virtually invisible. When I finally stepped back and looked at that room, perfectly seamless, *that's* when I felt good about myself. That precision, that skill... that's how I measure my worth. \n\nAnd my classes, too. I mean, I'm thirty-three, I'm sitting in these community college classrooms with kids fresh out of high school, and I'm pushing myself to the absolute limit to understand these complex accounting principles and business laws. When I finally get a spreadsheet to balance, or when I get an A on a midterm after studying at my kitchen table until two in the morning with my dry toast... that's what I care about. I want to be a successful business owner. I want to run my own contracting firm and have my own crews out there doing the manual labor while I manage the big picture. \n\nSo, no, I don't really sit around obsessing over my shape or judging my character based on my body. I just... I don't really have the time or the mental energy to care about something so superficial when I have a whole business to build, you know? It's just all about the work and the future for me right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself constantly thinking about food, weight, or body shape, even when you're trying to focus on something else, like your work or your schoolwork?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, I don't. I can't afford to be distracted by anything, let alone daydreaming about food or worrying about my waistline. \n\nTake yesterday, for example. I was doing this really intricate William Morris print in a half-bath for a client over in the Heights. I'm thinking about where the repeat in the pattern falls, how much drop I need to account for, making sure the plumb line is absolutely perfect because in those old houses, the corners are never, ever square. Never. If I were standing there obsessing over my body shape or thinking about a sandwich, I'd completely ruin a three-hundred-dollar roll of paper. I just have to be locked in.\n\nAnd then when I get home, it's straight into the books. I'm taking this managerial accounting class right now, and the professor is just brutal. We have this massive project due on cost-volume-profit analysis, and I'm sitting there trying to calculate break-even points for this hypothetical manufacturing company. It takes all my concentration. I'll sit there for three, maybe four hours straight just staring at Excel cells, trying to figure out where I missed a decimal point or why my liabilities aren't matching my assets. \n\nSo, no, food just doesn't cross my mind when I'm doing all of that. I'm thinking about where the repeat in the pattern falls, how much drop I need to account for, making sure the plumb line is absolutely perfect because in those old houses, the corners are never, ever square. Never. If I were standing there obsessing over my body shape or thinking about a sandwich, I'd completely ruin a three-hundred-dollar roll of paper. I just have to be locked in.\n\nAnd then when I get home, it's straight into the books. I'm taking this managerial accounting class right now, and the professor is just brutal. We have this massive project due on cost-volume-profit analysis, and I'm sitting there trying to calculate break-even points for this hypothetical manufacturing company. It takes all my concentration. I'll sit there for three, maybe four hours straight just staring at Excel cells, trying to figure out where I missed a decimal point or why my liabilities aren't matching my assets. \n\nSo, no, food just doesn't cross my mind when I'm doing all of that. It’s the furthest thing from it. And my body shape? I don't even think about it unless my tool belt feels like it's shifting or something and I need to adjust it so my shears don't fall out. My mind is just... it's just always on the business, always on the next step. I have to stay focused. If I lose focus, I lose money, or I fail a class, and I just can't let that happen if I'm going to get my contractor's license next spring. So, no, I definitely wouldn't say I'm constantly thinking about those things. I'm just thinking about work.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your current eating habits are causing you any significant distress or are they interfering with your ability to function in any important area of your life, like socially, at work, or in school?\n\nPatient: I mean, as far as my actual responsibilities go, no, not at all. I am still showing up for every single job, usually fifteen minutes early to prep the walls and get my drop cloths laid out, and I haven't missed a single lecture in any of my classes. So the important stuff, the work and the school, that is all completely on track. But I guess if you are asking about the social side of things, like socializing at work or school... maybe a little? But it is not really distress, it is just me making choices to avoid a hassle. \n\nLike, I have started completely avoiding lunches with my coworkers or the other tradesmen on the job sites. Usually around noon, the drywall guys or the electricians will all gather around the tailgate of someone's truck, or they will do a big run to the local deli and bring back these massive, heavy sandwiches and sit around eating together. I used to sit with them, but lately it is just so much easier to go sit in my own van or just keep working through the break. Because if I sit there with my specific portion of crackers or my black coffee, somebody always has to make a comment. They always tell me I need to eat a real meal, or they ask why I am eating like a bird, or they offer to buy me food. They are just blue-collar guys being friendly, I know that, but it is incredibly annoying and it disrupts my focus. \n\nAnd it is the exact same situation at school. We have these study meetups for my accounting class, which you really need because the material is so dense and the practice sets take hours, but the group always wants to meet up at the diner near campus or they want to order pizzas to the library study rooms. I have just started making up excuses to skip them entirely. I will tell them I have a client call or I just study alone at my kitchen table instead. It makes learning the material a bit harder because I do not have anyone to bounce questions off of, but honestly, it just feels so much easier to keep my routine tight this way. When I am by myself, I can stick to my schedule, have exactly what I planned to have, and I do not have to deal with anyone analyzing my plate or commenting on what I am doing. So I am still functioning perfectly fine, I am just doing it a lot more independently now.\n\nDoctor: Would you say you have an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though you are already at a low weight?\n\nPatient: I mean, I wouldn't really call it a fear of becoming \"fat\" in, like, a cosmetic or vanity kind of way. I don't care about being on a magazine cover. But gaining weight? Yeah... yeah, I guess I do have a pretty intense fear of that. It’s just... it’s almost a physical reaction for me. \n\nIf I even think about eating something heavy, like the pizza those study groups always want to order, or one of those massive, heavy deli sandwiches the drywallers eat on the job site, I get this really intense, panicky feeling in my chest. I just start spiraling, thinking that if I actually sit down and eat that kind of food, I'll wake up the next morning bigger and slower. And in my line of work, being slow is basically a death sentence for your profit margins and your reputation. \n\nPeople really underestimate how athletic you have to be to do high-end wallpapering or custom painting. You're not just standing in one spot. You're constantly up and down a six-foot A-frame ladder, sometimes an extension ladder if you're dealing with a vaulted ceiling or a two-story foyer, which is incredibly dangerous if you aren't completely centered. You're carrying cumbersome rolls of paper, you're dodging buckets of paste, and you're constantly twisting and reaching. If I put on weight, if I get bigger, I just know I won't be able to move around the ladders and navigate these tight rooms the way I need to. \n\nYou have to be so incredibly agile to squeeze behind scaffolding or lean over a staircase railing just right to smooth a seam without tearing the paper. If I'm heavier and sluggish from eating all that dense food, I lose my edge. I lose my balance, my speed, my stamina... everything. I need to stay light on my feet so I can pivot and climb and stretch for eight or ten hours a day. So, yes, the thought of gaining weight absolutely terrifies me, it really makes me panic, but it's because of how it would completely ruin my ability to physically do my job and build my business.\n\nDoctor: Even though you don't primarily judge yourself by your body shape or weight, do you feel that your concerns about staying light for work affect how you see yourself overall?\n\nPatient: I don't... I mean, no, not really. I don't think it affects how I see myself as a person at all. The whole staying light thing, it's really just... it's just practical. It's just maintenance. Like, how I see myself overall is entirely based on my work ethic and my business. If you want to know how I judge myself, it's by looking at my calendar and seeing that I am booked solid for the next four months. It's by the fact that I have general contractors calling me specifically because they know I don't mess up high-end wallcoverings. \n\nLike, just the other day, this designer called me about a natural grasscloth installation. Grasscloth is notoriously unforgiving. If you get even a single drop of water or paste on the face of it, it stains permanently, and you can't wipe it off. You just have to rip down the whole strip and start over, and at a hundred and fifty bucks a yard, you simply cannot afford mistakes. And she called me because she knows I am meticulous. That's how I see myself—meticulous, driven, a professional. \n\nMy body is just... it's just a tool to get that job done. Just like my laser level or my favorite smoothing brush. You wouldn't judge your whole identity by the condition of your paintbrush, right? You just keep it clean and ready to work. So keeping myself light and agile, it doesn't mean anything about my worth or who I am, it's just making sure the equipment is functioning at peak capacity. My self-worth is tied to my grades in my accounting class, my profit margins, the fact that I'm building something from the ground up all by myself. \n\nI'm taking my midterms next week, actually, and I've been studying so incredibly hard for this managerial accounting exam because if I can pull an A, it bumps my GPA up enough to qualify for this small business grant I've been looking at for female entrepreneurs. That's what I care about. That's who I am. I'm a business owner. So, no, the weight thing is just a physical requirement of the trade, it doesn't seep into my actual identity or my self-esteem or anything like that. I'm just a contractor trying to get my license and run a profitable company, you know?\n\nDoctor: Do you sometimes see yourself as heavier or bigger than you actually are, even when others might not notice the same thing?\n\nPatient: I mean... no, not at all. I don't have that issue. I know exactly what size I am. I think my spatial awareness is actually, like, hyper-accurate, because it absolutely has to be for my job. I don't look in the mirror and see someone huge or anything like that. I just see me. Because, honestly, if I didn't know exactly how much space my physical body takes up, I would be a completely terrible paperhanger. \n\nLike, just last week, I was doing this incredibly cramped powder room under a set of stairs in this older colonial house. Well, I had to get behind this pedestal sink to smooth down this really delicate foil-backed wallpaper, and you have to know exactly how your shoulders and your hips are going to fit into that gap. If you misjudge it by even a fraction of an inch, you'll scrape the foil, crease it, and ruin the entire drop, and then you're out a lot of money and time. I knew I had exactly maybe seven or eight inches of clearance, and I knew my body could fit. If I was walking around thinking I was way bigger or heavier than I actually am, I wouldn't even attempt half the jobs I take on. I'd be second-guessing my movements all day long, and I just can't afford to do that. \n\nSo, no, I don't have some distorted funhouse mirror in my head. I see exactly what is there. My concern is just making sure that what is there stays exactly as it is, so I can keep fitting into those tight gaps and moving the way I need to. I need to be able to trust my measurements, whether it's the square footage of the wall or my own dimensions. So I definitely don't look at myself and see someone heavier. I just look at myself and think, okay, good, I'm still light enough to get up on the scaffolding today without the aluminum planks bowing, I'm still small enough to maneuver around the drop cloths without knocking over a tray of sizing primer. It's all very literal for me, very mathematical. I just don't imagine things that aren't there.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't primarily judge yourself by your body shape or weight, do you find that your concerns about your weight or shape influence how you feel about yourself overall, even in subtle ways?\n\nPatient: I mean, I know you're kind of asking the same thing again, but... no, honestly, not even in subtle ways. It's always, always about the work or my classes. \n\nLike, if I feel bad about myself, it’s because I underbid a job. That actually just happened last month. I was quoting this exterior paint job for a wrap-around porch on this older Victorian house—beautiful house, really ornate spindle work on the railings—and I totally underestimated how much time it would take to scrape the old, flaking paint safely. I had to set up all this heavy containment plastic, wear the respirator all day, use the special HEPA vacuums, and it took three extra days just for the prep work. I ended up practically paying them to work on their house because my labor costs completely ate up the entire profit margin. That made me feel terrible about myself. I felt so stupid, so amateurish, you know? I was just sitting in my truck afterward feeling like a complete failure as a business owner. \n\nAnd that's the kind of stuff that actually ruins my self-esteem. Not my weight. My weight is just... it's just a constant, like the weather. You just manage it so you can do the work. If I feel good about myself, on the flip side, it's because I nailed a midterm, or because I finally figured out how to balance my ledger in QuickBooks without having to email my accounting professor for help. I spend so many nights just sitting at my kitchen table, still covered in drywall dust and caulk, staring at spreadsheets until my eyes cross, just trying to make sure I'm actually building a sustainable company. Because that's what matters to me. I want to be the person general contractors call when they have a high-stakes project, like a tricky stairwell or an expensive mural. \n\nSo, no, if I look in the mirror, I'm not nitpicking my shape or feeling bad about my waistline or letting it subtly ruin my day. Because if I sit there with my specific portion of crackers or my black coffee, somebody always has to make a comment. They always tell me I need to eat a real meal, or they ask why I am eating like a bird, or they offer to buy me food. They are just blue-collar guys being friendly, I know that, but it is incredibly annoying and it disrupts my focus. \n\nAnd it is the exact same situation at school. We have these study meetups for my accounting class, which you really need because the material is so dense and the practice sets take hours, but the group always wants to meet up at the diner near campus or they want to order pizzas to the library study rooms. I have just started making up excuses to skip them entirely. I will tell them I have a client call or I just study alone at my kitchen table instead. It makes learning the material a bit harder because I do not have anyone to bounce questions off of, but honestly, it just feels so much easier to keep my routine tight this way. When I am by myself, I can stick to my schedule, have exactly what I planned to have, and I do not have to deal with anyone analyzing my plate or commenting on what I am doing. So I am still functioning perfectly fine, I am just doing it a lot more independently now.\n\nDoctor: Would you say you have an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though you are already at a low weight?\n\nPatient: I mean, I wouldn't really call it a fear of becoming \"fat\" in, like, a cosmetic or vanity kind of way. I don't care about being on a magazine cover. But gaining weight? Yeah... yeah, I guess I do have a pretty intense fear of that. It’s just... it’s almost a physical reaction for me. \n\nIf I even think about eating something heavy, like the pizza those study groups always want to order, or one of those massive, heavy deli sandwiches the drywallers eat on the job site, I get this really intense, panicky feeling in my chest. I just start spiraling, thinking that if I actually sit down and eat that kind of food, I'll wake up the next morning bigger and slower. And in my line of work, being slow is basically a death sentence for your profit margins and your reputation. \n\nPeople really underestimate how athletic you have to be to do high-end wallpapering or custom painting. You're not just standing in one spot. You're constantly up and down a six-foot A-frame ladder, sometimes an extension ladder if you're dealing with a vaulted ceiling or a two-story foyer, which is incredibly dangerous if you aren't completely centered. You're carrying cumbersome rolls of paper, you're dodging buckets of paste, and you're constantly twisting and reaching. If I put on weight, if I get bigger, I just know I won't be able to move around the ladders and navigate these tight rooms the way I need to. \n\nYou have to be so incredibly agile to squeeze behind scaffolding or lean over a staircase railing just right to smooth a seam without tearing the paper. If I'm heavier and sluggish from eating all that dense food, I lose my edge. I lose my balance, my speed, my stamina... everything. I need to stay light on my feet so I can pivot and climb and stretch for eight or ten hours a day. So, yes, the thought of gaining weight absolutely terrifies me, it really makes me panic, but it's because of how it would completely ruin my ability to physically do my job and build my business.\n\nDoctor: Even though you don't primarily judge yourself by your body shape or weight, do you feel that your concerns about staying light for work affect how you see yourself overall?\n\nPatient: I don't... I mean, no, not really. I don't think it affects how I see myself as a person at all. The whole staying light thing, it's really just... it's just practical. It's just maintenance. Like, how I see myself overall is entirely based on my work ethic and my business. If you want to know how I judge myself, it's by looking at my calendar and seeing that I am booked solid for the next four months. It's by the fact that I have general contractors calling me specifically because they know I don't mess up high-end wallcoverings. \n\nLike, just the other day, this designer called me about a natural grasscloth installation. Grasscloth is notoriously unforgiving. If you get even a single drop of water or paste on the face of it, it stains permanently, and you can't wipe it off. You just have to rip down the whole strip and start over, and at a hundred and fifty bucks a yard, you simply cannot afford mistakes. And she called me because she knows I am meticulous. That's how I see myself—meticulous, driven, a professional. \n\nMy body is just... it's just a tool to get that job done. Just like my laser level or my favorite smoothing brush. You wouldn't judge your whole identity by the condition of your paintbrush, right? You just keep it clean and ready to work. So keeping myself light and agile, it doesn't mean anything about my worth or who I am, it's just making sure the equipment is functioning at peak capacity. My self-worth is tied to my grades in my accounting class, my profit margins, the fact that I'm building something from the ground up all by myself. \n\nI'm taking my midterms next week, actually, and I've been studying so incredibly hard for this managerial accounting exam because if I can pull an A, it bumps my GPA up enough to qualify for this small business grant I've been looking at for female entrepreneurs. That's what I care about. That's who I am. I'm a business owner. So, no, the weight thing is just a physical requirement of the trade, it doesn't seep into my actual identity or my self-esteem or anything like that. I'm just a contractor trying to get my license and run a profitable company, you know?\n\nDoctor: Do you sometimes see yourself as heavier or bigger than you actually are, even when others might not notice the same thing?\n\nPatient: I mean... no, not at all. I don't have that issue. I know exactly what size I am. I think my spatial awareness is actually, like, hyper-accurate, because it absolutely has to be for my job. I don't look in the mirror and see someone huge or anything like that. I just see me. I knew I had exactly maybe seven or eight inches of clearance, and I knew my body could fit. If I was walking around thinking I was way bigger or heavier than I actually am, I wouldn't even attempt half the jobs I take on. I'd be second-guessing my movements all day long, and I just can't afford to do that. \n\nSo, no, I don't have some distorted funhouse mirror in my head. I see exactly what is there. My concern is just making sure that what is there stays exactly as it is, so I can keep fitting into those tight gaps and moving the way I need to. I need to be able to trust my measurements, whether it's the square footage of the wall or my own dimensions. So I definitely don't look at myself and see someone heavier. I just look at myself and think, okay, good, I'm still light enough to get up on the scaffolding today without the aluminum planks bowing, I'm still small enough to maneuver around the drop cloths without knocking over a tray of sizing primer. It's all very literal for me, very mathematical. I just don't imagine things that aren't there.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't primarily judge yourself by your body shape or weight, do you find that your concerns about your weight or shape influence how you feel about yourself overall, even in subtle ways?\n\nPatient: I mean, I know you're kind of asking the same thing again, but... no, honestly, not even in subtle ways. It really doesn't. If I'm having a bad day where I feel awful about myself, it has absolutely zero to do with my body or my weight or anything like that. It's always, always about the work or my classes. \n\nLike, if I feel bad about myself, it’s because I underbid a job. That actually just happened last month. I was quoting this exterior paint job for a wrap-around porch on this older Victorian house—beautiful house, really ornate spindle work on the railings—and I totally underestimated how much time it would take to scrape the old, flaking paint safely. I had to set up all this heavy containment plastic, wear the respirator all day, use the special HEPA vacuums, and it took three extra days just for the prep work. I ended up practically paying them to work on their house because my labor costs completely ate up the entire profit margin. That made me feel terrible about myself. I felt so stupid, so amateurish, you know? I was just sitting in my truck afterward feeling like a complete failure as a business owner. \n\nAnd that's the kind of stuff that actually ruins my self-esteem. Not my weight. I spend so many nights just sitting at my kitchen table, still covered in drywall dust and caulk, staring at spreadsheets until my eyes cross, just trying to make sure I'm actually building a sustainable company. Can I cut a straight line against a ceiling without using painter's tape? Yes. Can I hang fifty yards of delicate paper without a single visible seam? Yes. That's who I am. Like I was trying to explain earlier, it's practically a job requirement to know your exact mass and dimensions, so my perception of my body is completely tethered to reality. \n\nJust to give you another example, because I really want you to understand how practical this is for me—last Tuesday, I was doing this massive drywall repair and ceiling skim coat in a two-story foyer. High-gloss shows every single microscopic imperfection, so you have to float the joints flawlessly. The plank has a load limit, sure, but when you factor in a five-gallon bucket of joint compound—which weighs about sixty pounds on its own—plus the mud pan, the twelve-inch taping knives, my work boots... you have to do the math. I step out onto the center of that board and it barely even flexes. I don't stand up there feeling big or heavy. I mean, I feel like I’m sort of repeating myself here, doctor, because we literally just talked about this a few minutes ago. But just to be absolutely, one hundred percent clear on the performance side of things: no. It does not interfere with my actual work. My performance is flawless.
